sections.h2: How does an eviction work in a Kentucky court?
sections.html:
A Kentucky eviction is a forcible detainer case filed in the District Court of the county where the property sits. KRS 383.200 defines a forcible detainer to include a tenant's refusal to give the landlord possession after the term ends, and KRS 383.210 says the court issues a warrant to the sheriff or a constable after the landlord files a complaint.

There is no eviction by the landlord's own hand. The case runs through the court from the first filing to the order that puts the owner back in possession, and a landlord who skips the court runs into the self-help ban in KRS 383.690.

sections.h2: What are the steps from the complaint to getting the house back?
sections.html:
The steps follow the statutes in order. Each one has a short deadline, so a landlord who prepares the paperwork before filing saves weeks.

Forcible detainer steps in KRS 383.200 to 383.285
StepWhat happensStatute
ComplaintLandlord files in District Court and a warrant goes to the sheriff or a constableKRS 383.210
ServiceEach defendant gets notice of the time and place at least three days ahead; without notice, no inquiry proceeds against that defendantKRS 383.210, 383.215
TrialThe court tries the case unless a party demands a juryKRS 383.210(2)
JudgmentRestitution of the premises and costs for the landlord, or costs for the defendantsKRS 383.240
Appeal windowSeven days after the findingKRS 383.255
Warrant of restitutionIf no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues the warrant on requestKRS 383.245

sections.h2: How much time does a tenant have to appeal, and what must be paid?
sections.html:
Either side has seven days from the finding to file an appeal. A tenant who appeals must put the rent already owing from the start of the case, and each later month's rent as it comes due, with the circuit court clerk.

The deposit stays with the clerk until the court orders distribution at the end of the appeal. Once the appeal is perfected by that payment, proceedings on the inquisition stop and the papers go up to the circuit court within ten days. If the appellant fails to pursue the appeal, KRS 383.260 makes the appellant and surety liable for the landlord's damages for the delay and for the reasonable cost of defending the appeal.

sections.h2: What if the occupant was never a tenant?
sections.html:
A 2025 statute, KRS 383.290, lets an owner ask law enforcement to remove a person who is unlawfully in the property, but only under tight conditions. It does not apply to a current or former tenant or to anyone who once had an agreement with the owner to occupy the premises.

  • The occupant is not and never was a tenant and never had an agreement from the owner.
  • The property was not open to the public when the occupant entered.
  • The owner has told the occupant to leave.
  • The occupant is not an immediate family member, and no litigation about the property is pending between them.

The owner presents a signed petition, the officer verifies identity and serves a notice to vacate, and the sheriff or constable may charge a $20 service fee. A person wrongfully removed has 60 days to sue in District Court and can recover attorney's fees, so use this route only when every condition fits.

sections.h2: What can a landlord do to speed the process, and what is off limits?
sections.html:
A landlord can file promptly, serve every named occupant and bring complete records. A landlord cannot change locks, remove doors or cut utilities. KRS 383.690 says a landlord may not take possession by action or otherwise, including interrupting heat, electric, water, gas or any other essential service.

  • Do not accept rent after serving a termination notice unless you intend to keep the tenancy alive. KRS 383.675 treats acceptance with knowledge of a default as a waiver of that breach.
  • Do not threaten a case or raise rent in response to a code complaint. KRS 383.705 presumes retaliation for complaints made within a year.
  • After termination, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent plus a separate claim for actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3).

sections.h2: How long does a landlord have to start a Kentucky eviction case?
sections.html:
KRS 383.285 bars an inquisition of forcible entry or detainer more than two years after the entry or detainer complained of. That is the outer limit, and the practical window is far shorter.

For a holdover past the end of a lease term outside URLTA areas, KRS 383.160 lets possession be recovered without demand or notice if proceedings start within 90 days of a term of a year or more, or within 30 days of a shorter term. Waiting past those periods pushes the next permitted filing back, so landlords should file quickly after a lease ends.

sections.h2: What costs and damages can a landlord recover?
sections.html:
The judgment for the landlord restores possession and awards the costs of the case. KRS 383.240 states the form: restitution of the premises plus costs expended, or costs for the defendants if they prevail.

Money claims are separate. After a termination under the URLTA, KRS 383.685 allows a claim for possession and rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant's willful noncompliance can support actual damages and attorney's fees under KRS 383.660(3). Keep rent ledgers, repair invoices and photographs so those amounts can be proved at trial.

sections.h2: How does a pending eviction affect selling the house?
sections.html:
A pending case does not stop a sale, but it changes who delivers possession. KRS 383.600 relieves a landlord who conveys in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser from liability under the rental agreement for events after written notice of the conveyance, unless the parties agreed otherwise.

Buyers and lenders often want the tenant gone before closing, so the contract should say who handles the case, who pays the costs and what happens if the judgment is appealed. Tenants must permit entry for showings on at least two days' notice at reasonable times under KRS 383.615, which gives a seller a lawful way to show an occupied house.

  • Get the case number, judgment and any warrant of restitution into the sale file.
  • Confirm whether any rent is sitting with the circuit court clerk after an appeal.
  • Ask the title company whether the occupancy affects the closing date.

sections.h2: Where can a Kentucky landlord find court forms and help?
sections.html:
Start with the District Court clerk in the county where the house sits, and ask for the current forcible detainer forms and filing fee. The Kentucky Court of Justice also runs a Legal Self-Help section on its website.

A real estate attorney can confirm which notice rules apply in your city and how a pending case should be handled in the sale contract. Ask the clerk, too, how the court wants service on each occupant arranged with the sheriff's office.

faqs.q: Which court handles evictions in Kentucky?
faqs.a: The District Court of the county where the property sits. The landlord files a forcible detainer complaint and the court issues a warrant to the sheriff or a constable under KRS 383.210.

faqs.q: How long does a tenant have to appeal an eviction judgment in Kentucky?
faqs.a: Seven days from the court's finding. The appealing party must deposit the rent owing and each later month's rent with the circuit court clerk.

faqs.q: Can a landlord lock out a tenant or turn off utilities?
faqs.a: No. KRS 383.690 forbids recovering possession by interrupting heat, electric, water, gas or other essential service. Possession comes through the court.

faqs.q: Does a sheriff remove a tenant after the judgment?
faqs.a: Yes. If no appeal is filed by the seventh day, the court issues a warrant of restitution on request, which directs the sheriff or constable to put the landlord in possession.

faqs.q: Can I use the quick removal process for a former tenant?
faqs.a: No. KRS 383.290 does not apply to a current or former tenant or anyone who once had an agreement to occupy the home. Those cases go through forcible detainer.
